Key findings

  • Overall conversion 3.7% is above the Dynamic Yield global average (2.66%), but it is carried by desktop (6.2%). Mobile converts at 2.2%, only 35% of desktop, while mobile is 61% of sessions.
  • Biggest single leak: mobile bag → checkout. Only 35% of mobile shoppers with something in the bag start checkout, vs 64% on desktop (mobile cart abandonment 70%).
  • Small baskets: 1.24 items per order vs 2.91 for the weakest DY industry (fashion). 41% of orders pay shipping, and 20% land just under the €100 free-shipping threshold (€70–100).
  • Mobile product pages turn fewer views into add-to-bag in every category (5–7.5% vs 7.6–13.9% on desktop).
  • Checkout itself performs well (81% of started checkouts complete, above the 66% top-10% benchmark). Search returns zero results in 15% of searches (all for 'tent').

Sources: Dynamic Yield e-commerce benchmarks · Videowise: Ecommerce conversion funnel benchmarks (Aug 2026)

Step 2 · Test hypotheses

Ranked by ICE (Impact · Confidence · Ease, 1–10). Basis: a gap against benchmarks, or established best practice. Designs per hypothesis: Test designs.

H2Benchmark gapICE 7·7·9 = 441

Free-shipping progress bar in the bag

Observation. 1.24 items per order (benchmark 2.9). 41% of orders pay shipping and 20% fall just under the €100 free-shipping threshold.

Hypothesis. Because many baskets end just below €100, we believe showing progress towards free shipping ('€18 to free shipping') in the bag will make shoppers add another item, raising items per order and revenue per visitor.

Change. Progress bar with the remaining amount at the top of the slide-in bag and cart; turns green with 'Free shipping unlocked' at €100.

Page: Slide-in bag + cartDevices: allPrimary: revenue per visitor (cart visitors)Guardrails: purchaseStatus: proposed
H1Benchmark gapICE 8·6·8 = 384

Mobile bag: make checkout the obvious next step

Observation. Only 35% of mobile shoppers with a full bag start checkout vs 64% on desktop; mobile cart abandonment is 70%.

Hypothesis. Because mobile shoppers see a long bag with the Checkout button pushed down and no reassurance, we believe a sticky Checkout button with delivery and returns reassurance in the bag will raise mobile checkout starts.

Change. Sticky footer in the slide-in bag on mobile: subtotal, prominent Checkout button, and a line with '30-day free returns · delivery in 1–2 days'.

Page: Slide-in bag (mobile)Devices: mobilePrimary: begin_checkout (mobile sessions with add-to-cart)Guardrails: purchase, rpvStatus: proposed
H4Best practiceICE 6·5·8 = 240

Sticky Add to bag on mobile product pages

Observation. Mobile product pages convert views to add-to-bag at 5–7.5% vs 7.6–13.9% on desktop, in every category. Product pages are now long (copy, specs, reviews).

Hypothesis. Because mobile shoppers scroll into copy, specs and reviews and lose the Add to bag button, we believe a sticky Add to bag bar (price + button) that appears once the main button scrolls away will raise mobile add-to-bag rate.

Change. Bottom sticky bar on mobile PDPs with product name, price and Add to bag, shown when the main button is out of view; asks for size if none selected.

Page: Product page (mobile)Devices: mobilePrimary: add_to_cart (mobile PDP visitors)Guardrails: purchase, rpvStatus: proposed
H3Benchmark gapICE 7·5·6 = 210

'Complete your kit' on product pages

Observation. Baskets are small (1.24 items) and accessories are cheap add-ons (€31–65) that rarely get added alongside jackets, boots and packs.

Hypothesis. Because shoppers buying a main item are not shown matching accessories, we believe a 'Complete your kit' row with quick add will raise items per order.

Change. Row of 3 matching accessories under Add to bag, each with image, price, stars and a quick '+ Add' button.

Page: Product pageDevices: allPrimary: items per order / revenue per visitorGuardrails: add_to_cart, purchaseStatus: proposed
H5Best practiceICE 3·8·8 = 192

Helpful zero-result search page

Observation. 15% of searches return nothing (all for 'tent'), and those sessions end with a dead-end 'No products found'.

Hypothesis. Because a dead-end search page gives shoppers nowhere to go, we believe suggesting related categories and popular products on zero-result searches will keep them browsing and raise product views from search.

Change. Zero-result page with 'We don't sell tents yet', links to related categories (Backpacks, Accessories) and a row of 4 bestsellers.

Page: Search resultsDevices: allPrimary: view_item (search sessions)Guardrails: purchaseStatus: proposed

Experiments

Primary-metric results per variant among exposed visitors. "Preview" opens the live shop in that variant (not tracked). Green = significant win at α = 0.01.

Decision rules

Fixed in advance; the engine cannot ship a change that fails them.

Min. exposed visitors per variant400
Max. per variant (then stop)4000
Significance level α0.01
Min. probability to beat control0.95
SRM alarm p0.001
Guardrail harm α0.1
Max. concurrent tests3
  1. R1 Validity: if the sample-ratio-mismatch p-value < srm_p_threshold the test is INVALID — pause and investigate, never ship.
  2. R2 Patience: no decision before every variant has min_exposed_per_variant exposed visitors. alpha is 0.01 (not 0.05) because results are checked after every traffic run (sequential peeking).
  3. R3 Ship: primary metric uplift > min_relative_uplift, two-sided p < alpha AND probability-to-beat-control >= min_prob_to_beat.
  4. R4 Guardrails: do not ship if any guardrail metric is worse with p < guardrail_harm_alpha, or its point estimate drops more than guardrail_max_relative_drop (sanity cap) — unless the primary metric IS that guardrail.
  5. R5 Kill: stop if the primary metric is significantly worse (p < alpha), or max_exposed_per_variant is reached without a ship decision (inconclusive -> keep control: simplest wins).
  6. R6 Isolation: at most max_concurrent_experiments running, and never two running experiments that change the same feature key or share an exposure page.
  7. R7 Ship = merge the winning variant's features/css into site/config/site-config.json, log to docs/decision-log.md; the change becomes the new control.
